On the half decayed veranda of a small wooden house near the edge of a ravine, outside Winesburg, Ohio, a fat little old man walked nervously up and down. <break time="0.8s" /> Beyond a long field, where clover had been planted but only yellow mustard weeds had grown, he could see the highway and a wagon full of berry pickers coming home. <break time="0.8s" /> The young men and women in the wagon laughed and shouted noisily, and a girls voice called to him, Oh, you Wing Biddlebaum, comb your hair. <break time="0.8s" /> The man was bald, yet his nervous little hands fluttered about his bare white forehead as though he were arranging a mass of tangled hair. <break time="0.8s" /> Wing Biddlebaum had lived in Winesburg for twenty years, but he did not think of himself as a part of the life of the town. <break time="0.8s" /> He was always frightened and troubled by a ghostly crowd of doubts, and among all the people of Winesburg, only one had ever come close to him. <break time="0.8s" /> That one was George Willard, a young reporter on the town newspaper, the Winesburg Eagle, with whom Wing had formed something like a friendship. <break time="0.8s" /> Now, as the sun went down, the old man walked up and down the veranda, hoping that George would come and spend the evening with him.

With George Willard beside him, Wing lost some of his timidity, and the shadowy self usually buried under his doubts came out to look at the world. <break time="0.8s" /> When he talked with the young reporter, his voice, which had been low and trembling, became loud and sharp, and his bent body straightened. <break time="0.8s" /> Then his slender, expressive fingers would begin to beat upon a table or the top board of a fence, and this seemed to make him more comfortable. <break time="0.8s" /> The story of Wing Biddlebaum is a story of hands, and their restless activity, like the beating wings of a caged bird, had given him his name. <break time="0.8s" /> Wing tried to keep his hands hidden, and he looked with wonder at the quiet hands of other men who worked beside him in the fields. <break time="0.8s" /> In Winesburg the hands had attracted attention merely because of their activity, and with them he had once picked as many as a hundred and forty quarts of strawberries in a day. <break time="0.8s" /> The town was proud of his hands in the same way that it was proud of Banker Whites new stone house and Wesley Moyers trotting stallion, Tony Tip. <break time="0.8s" /> Although George Willard had often felt a strong curiosity about the hands, only his growing respect for the old man had kept him from asking.

Earlier that summer afternoon. <break time="0.8s" /> The two had walked together in the fields. <break time="0.8s" /> And when they sat down on a grassy bank. <break time="0.8s" /> Wing spoke with a sudden, eager passion. <break time="0.8s" /> You are destroying yourself, he cried. <break time="0.8s" /> Because you are too much influenced. <break time="0.8s" /> By the people in this town. <break time="0.8s" /> And you are afraid of your own dreams. <break time="0.8s" /> You must try to forget all you have learned, Wing said. <break time="0.8s" /> And from now on you must shut your ears. <break time="0.8s" /> To the roaring voices around you. <break time="0.8s" /> Then, with his voice growing soft. <break time="0.8s" /> He painted a picture of a golden age. <break time="0.8s" /> In which young men came across the green countryside. <break time="0.8s" /> Some on foot and some on horses. <break time="0.8s" /> They gathered at the feet of an old man. <break time="0.8s" /> Who sat beneath a tree in a tiny garden. <break time="0.8s" /> And they listened eagerly to his words. <break time="0.8s" /> As he talked. <break time="0.8s" /> Wing forgot his hands. <break time="0.8s" /> And slowly they crept forward. <break time="0.8s" /> And came to rest on George Willards shoulders. <break time="0.8s" /> Suddenly a look of horror. <break time="0.8s" /> Swept over his face. <break time="0.8s" /> And jumping to his feet. <break time="0.8s" /> He thrust his hands deep into his pockets. <break time="0.8s" /> While tears came into his eyes. <break time="0.8s" /> I must go home now. <break time="0.8s" /> And I cannot talk with you any longer. <break time="0.8s" /> He said nervously. <break time="0.8s" /> And he hurried away across the meadow. <break time="0.8s" /> Without looking back. <break time="0.8s" /> Leaving the young man puzzled and afraid.
